editorial.title: 동맹 신뢰로 풀어야 할 전작권 전환 ‘조건’ 이견
editorial.body: ① 한국 정부가 내년 전작권 전환 시점을 못 박으려 하자 주한미군사령관은 조건 변화를 들어 반대했습니다. ② 정부는 다음 달 한미안보협의회의에서 전환 로드맵을 확정하려 하지만 일정조차 잡지 못했습니다. ③ 북한 위협과 전장 환경 변화가 거론되면서 전환 조건 논쟁이 커졌고 전작권 전환은 동맹 신뢰로 풀어야 한다고 지적했습니다.

editorial.titleTr: Alliance Trust Key to Resolving Conditions for Wartime Operational Control Transfer Disagreement
summaryTr: South Korean government pushes to fix timing of wartime operational control transfer next year vs. U.S. military commander opposes changing conditions
North Korean threats and changing battlefield environment intensify debate over transfer conditions, South Korea-U.S. security consultative meeting schedule remains undecided
Wartime operational control transfer should be resolved based on alliance trust rather than schedule, experts note
editorial.bodyTr: The South Korean government attempted to set a specific timeline for the transfer of wartime operational control next year, but the commander of United States Forces Korea opposed it citing changed circumstances. The government sought to finalize a transition roadmap at the Korea-U.S. Security Consultative Meeting next month, but has not even been able to schedule the meeting. As North Korean threats and changes in the battlefield environment were raised, the debate over transition conditions intensified, with experts pointing out that the transfer of wartime operational control must be resolved through strengthened alliance trust.

summaryTr: KOSPI plummets to the 5000s from 9300 in four months, widening investor losses.
Experts point to leveraged ETFs and pension rebalancing as factors amplifying the decline.
Concerns mount over government and pension funds delaying disclosure of decision-making processes and shirking responsibility.
editorials.bodyTr: The KOSPI has plummeted from the 9,300 level to the mid-5,000s in just four months, inflicting substantial losses on investors. The article points out that single-stock leveraged ETFs and the postponement of the National Pension Service's rebalancing have amplified the scale of the decline. With the government and the National Pension Service delaying the release of decision-making materials and falling short of clarifying responsibility, concerns about a recurrence have grown.

summaryTr: The National Pension Service missed its opportunity to sell at market peaks.
It lost its role as a safety net for the stock market during the sharp decline.
Lack of transparency raises concerns due to its non-public operations.
editorial.bodyTr: The National Pension Service has missed opportunities to sell at market peaks and increased its domestic stock allocation, losing its function as a market safety valve during sharp declines. editorial.titleTr: [Editorial] Wartime Command Transfer Faces Friction; Confidence Alone Won't Suffice
summaryTr: U.S. Maintains 'Conditions Not Met' Stance in Assessment of South Korea's Full Operational Capability for OPCON Transfer
Discontent Over 'Moving the Goalposts' as Items Met Last Year Are Re-evaluated as Unmet This Year
Bridging Military-to-Military Differences and Restoring Trust Take Priority Over Political Agreement
editorial.bodyTr:
The United States is maintaining its position that conditions remain unmet regarding verification of full operational capability (FOC) necessary for South Korea to assume wartime operational control (OPCON). The government had envisioned completing verification this year and establishing a target date for transition, but it now faces an impasse at the first hurdle due to diverging views between Seoul and Washington. General Xavier Brunson, commander of U.S. Forces Korea, warned on the 12th during a discussion at the Center for Strategic and International Studies that "time is also a condition," cautioning that a transition without adequate capabilities could undermine defensive strength.

The problem is that the United States has now deemed some items it previously evaluated as "met" last year to be "unmet" this year. This explains complaints from the South Korean military that the United States is "moving the goalposts." According to reports, the U.S. position is that previously met items must be reassessed annually as the battlefield environment evolves. The U.S. is particularly concerned with surveillance and reconnaissance assets and command-and-control systems. The demands reportedly include improving data links and communication security systems to operate in conjunction with Maven, an artificial intelligence-based targeting analysis system used in actual operations, and ensuring the future combined command headquarters to be led by a South Korean general possesses corresponding capabilities.

On the surface, this represents how rapid advances in AI utilization and new weapons systems in military operations have emerged as a wild card in OPCON negotiations. However, this is precisely the kind of issue that can be resolved through close coordination at the working level. The reason OPCON transition, a matter on which both nations have already set timelines, is encountering such friction must be soberly examined: there is a fundamental erosion of mutual trust between the two sides. President Lee Jae-myung stated in May that "even if OPCON is recovered tomorrow, there would be no problem," and the Defense Ministry has maintained that there are no major disagreements between Seoul and Washington. However, if FOC verification cannot even be completed, the transition cannot be accelerated through confidence alone. There are observations that Seoul is delaying the Korea-U.S. Security Consultative Meeting schedule to secure time to persuade Washington and is seeking a "top-down" resolution between leaders through political agreement.

Rather than rushing toward political accord, priority should be given to narrowing disagreements between military authorities regarding evaluation criteria and transition conditions. OPCON transition is a task that must be accomplished for autonomous defense. However, if it is not backed by the establishment of operational capabilities for our military and close communication between Seoul and Washington, public security concerns will only grow.

editorial.title: Chip vulnerability
editorial.body: Record tech profits obscure the structural fragility of Korea’s single-engine economy Economic success can conceal the cost of economic dependence. South Korea offers a case in point: A semiconductor boom has raised growth forecasts and delivered record corporate earnings, yet its stock market has been gripped by panic, with repeated trading halts. The disconnect, even as Samsung Electronics reported unprecedented quarterly operating profits last week, points to a structural weakness in an economy whose fortunes rest too heavily on a single industry. The sell-off reflects several converging pressures: Renewed US inflation concerns have unsettled interest-rate expectations, doubts have emerged over the financing of artificial intelligence infrastructure, and Chinese memory chip-makers are challenging assumptions about Korea’s technological lead. Taken together, these developments illustrate the vulnerability of a growth model tethered to global demand for memory chips. Hotter US inflation data has revived fears that borrowing costs will remain elevated, weighing on technology shares worldwide. Rising bond yields for AI infrastructure provider CoreWeave have added to the unease. Its financing arrangements and close commercial ties with Nvidia have drawn scrutiny to the circular relationships underpinning parts of the AI investment boom. If expensive credit forces major technology companies to curb infrastructure spending, memory demand could weaken sooner than Korean producers anticipate. Record profits offer little shelter when the market begins to question what comes next. China poses a longer-term challenge. ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, has announced plans to introduce server DRAM using a new architecture, which reduces memory-cell area by roughly one-third compared with the conventional design. Yet its commercial production at competitive yields remains uncertain, and the announcement does not prove that Chinese manufacturers have overtaken their Korean rivals. However, treating the claim as mere publicity would be complacent. China has repeatedly deployed state-backed investment and alternative technological approaches to challenge established industrial leaders. Its strategy can involve changing the terms of competition rather than simply copying the incumbent’s methods. Memory chips may prove harder to disrupt than telecommunications equipment or electric vehicles, but Korea cannot assume its lead will endure. The market reaction also reflects a domestic weakness. Semiconductor earnings dominate expectations for corporate profits, exports and growth. When confidence in the sector falters, the shock spreads across the economy. Other manufacturing pillars offer limited reassurance. Petrochemicals and steel face pressure from Chinese overcapacity and trade barriers, while electric vehicle makers confront aggressive foreign competition and shifting industrial policies. The Korea Development Institute has warned that Korea could enter a period of negative growth around 2030 if its long-term decline in growth potential continues. That warning deserves more attention than another upward revision to the annual growth forecast. Export windfalls can inflate headline figures without reversing weak productivity or creating durable sources of demand. Building expansive spending plans around semiconductor-related tax revenue would compound the danger if the boom fades. Fiscal policy should preserve room to respond to future shocks rather than treat an exceptional revenue cycle as a permanent funding source. Structural reform cannot wait for the next downturn. The Korean government should remove unnecessary barriers to corporate investment, make labor markets more adaptable, and open a greater scope for new businesses to challenge established players. It should also help capital and talent move into promising industries beyond semiconductors while maintaining fiscal discipline. A stock market rout cannot diversify an economy. It can expose the price of failing to do so. Korea’s semiconductor boom has bought time, but that reprieve will matter only if policymakers and businesses use it to build a broader base of productive activity. When the chip cycle turns, the strength of that foundation will count for more than the profits that preceded it. 미국의 높아진 인플레이션 데이터가 차입 비용이 높은 수준에 머물 수 있다는 우려를 되살렸고, 이는 전 세계 기술주를 압박하고 있다. 인공지능 인프라 제공업체인 코어위브의 채권 수익률 상승이 불안감을 더했다. 이 회사의 자금 조달 체계와 엔비디아와의 밀접한 상업 관계는 인공지능 투자 붐을 뒷받침하는 순환적 관계에 대한 감시를 초래했다. 만약 높은 차입 비용이 주요 기술 기업들의 인프라 지출을 억제한다면, 메모리 수요는 한국 제조사들의 예상보다 일찍 약해질 수 있다. 기록적인 수익도 시장이 다음에 어떤 일이 일어날지 의문을 품기 시작하면 보호막이 되지 못한다.

중국은 장기적 도전 과제다. 창신메모리테크놀로지는 새로운 아키텍처를 사용한 서버 디램 도입 계획을 발표했으며, 이는 기존 설계 대비 메모리셀 면적을 약 3분의 1 줄인다. 그러나 경쟁력 있는 수율로의 양산 가능성은 여전히 불확실하며, 이 발표만으로는 중국 제조사들이 한국 경쟁사를 능가했다는 것을 증명하지 못한다. 다만 이 주장을 단순한 홍보로 취급하는 것은 자만이다. 중국은 국가 지원 투자와 대안적 기술 접근을 반복해 기존 산업 지도자들에게 도전해왔다. 그 전략은 기존 기업의 방식을 단순히 모방하기보다는 경쟁의 조건 자체를 바꾸는 것을 수반할 수 있다. 메모리칩은 통신장비나 전기자동차보다는 파괴하기 어려울 수 있지만, 한국은 자신의 주도권이 지속될 것이라 가정할 수 없다.

시장 반응은 국내 약점도 반영한다. 반도체 수익이 기업 이익, 수출, 성장에 대한 기대를 지배한다. 해당 산업에 대한 신뢰가 흔들리면, 충격이 전체 경제로 퍼진다. 다른 제조업 기둥은 안심할 여지가 적다. 석유화학과 철강은 중국의 과잉 생산과 무역 장벽으로부터 압력을 받고 있으며, 전기자동차 제조사들은 공격적인 외국 경쟁과 변화하는 산업 정책에 직면해 있다. 한국개발연구원은 장기 성장 잠재력의 감소가 계속되면 한국이 2030년 무렵 마이너스 성장에 진입할 수 있다고 경고했다. 이 경고는 연간 성장 전망의 또 다른 상향 조정보다 더 많은 관심을 받을 가치가 있다.

수출 특수는 약한 생산성이나 지속 가능한 수요원을 역전시키지 못하면서 주요 지표를 부풀릴 수 있다. 반도체 관련 세수를 중심으로 대규모 지출 계획을 세우면, 호황이 사라질 경우 위험을 가중시킨다. 재정 정책은 예외적인 세수 사이클을 영구적인 재원으로 취급하기보다는 향후 충격에 대응할 여지를 유지해야 한다.

구조 개혁은 다음 경기 침체를 기다릴 수 없다. 한국 정부는 기업 투자에 대한 불필요한 장벽을 제거하고, 노동 시장의 적응력을 높이고, 기존 기업에 도전할 새로운 사업에 더 큰 기회를 제공해야 한다. 또한 재정 규율을 유지하면서 반도체를 넘어 유망한 산업으로 자본과 인재가 이동하도록 돕고, 다른 제조업 기둥을 강화해야 한다. 주식시장의 폭락은 경제를 다각화할 수 없다. 그것을 하지 못한 대가를 드러낼 수 있을 뿐이다. 한국의 반도체 호황이 시간을 벌어줬지만, 그 유예 기간이 의미를 가지려면 정책 입안자들과 기업들이 더 광범위한 생산 활동의 기반을 구축하는 데 그것을 사용해야 한다. 칩 사이클이 바뀔 때, 그 기반의 강도가 그 이전의 수익보다 훨씬 중요할 것이다.

editorials.title: Chip vulnerability
editorials.body: Record tech profits obscure the structural fragility of Korea’s single-engine economy Economic success can conceal the cost of economic dependence. South Korea offers a case in point: A semiconductor boom has raised growth forecasts and delivered record corporate earnings, yet its stock market has been gripped by panic, with repeated trading halts. The disconnect, even as Samsung Electronics reported unprecedented quarterly operating profits last week, points to a structural weakness in an economy whose fortunes rest too heavily on a single industry. The sell-off reflects several converging pressures: Renewed US inflation concerns have unsettled interest-rate expectations, doubts have emerged over the financing of artificial intelligence infrastructure, and Chinese memory chip-makers are challenging assumptions about Korea’s technological lead. Taken together, these developments illustrate the vulnerability of a growth model tethered to global demand for memory chips. Hotter US inflation data has revived fears that borrowing costs will remain elevated, weighing on technology shares worldwide. Rising bond yields for AI infrastructure provider CoreWeave have added to the unease. Its financing arrangements and close commercial ties with Nvidia have drawn scrutiny to the circular relationships underpinning parts of the AI investment boom. If expensive credit forces major technology companies to curb infrastructure spending, memory demand could weaken sooner than Korean producers anticipate. Record profits offer little shelter when the market begins to question what comes next. China poses a longer-term challenge. ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, has announced plans to introduce server DRAM using a new architecture, which reduces memory-cell area by roughly one-third compared with the conventional design. Yet its commercial production at competitive yields remains uncertain, and the announcement does not prove that Chinese manufacturers have overtaken their Korean rivals. However, treating the claim as mere publicity would be complacent. China has repeatedly deployed state-backed investment and alternative technological approaches to challenge established industrial leaders. Its strategy can involve changing the terms of competition rather than simply copying the incumbent’s methods. Memory chips may prove harder to disrupt than telecommunications equipment or electric vehicles, but Korea cannot assume its lead will endure. The market reaction also reflects a domestic weakness. Semiconductor earnings dominate expectations for corporate profits, exports and growth. When confidence in the sector falters, the shock spreads across the economy. Other manufacturing pillars offer limited reassurance. Petrochemicals and steel face pressure from Chinese overcapacity and trade barriers, while electric vehicle makers confront aggressive foreign competition and shifting industrial policies. The Korea Development Institute has warned that Korea could enter a period of negative growth around 2030 if its long-term decline in growth potential continues. That warning deserves more attention than another upward revision to the annual growth forecast. Export windfalls can inflate headline figures without reversing weak productivity or creating durable sources of demand. Building expansive spending plans around semiconductor-related tax revenue would compound the danger if the boom fades. Fiscal policy should preserve room to respond to future shocks rather than treat an exceptional revenue cycle as a permanent funding source. Structural reform cannot wait for the next downturn. The Korean government should remove unnecessary barriers to corporate investment, make labor markets more adaptable, and open a greater scope for new businesses to challenge established players. It should also help capital and talent move into promising industries beyond semiconductors while maintaining fiscal discipline. A stock market rout cannot diversify an economy. It can expose the price of failing to do so. Korea’s semiconductor boom has bought time, but that reprieve will matter only if policymakers and businesses use it to build a broader base of productive activity. When the chip cycle turns, the strength of that foundation will count for more than the profits that preceded it. editorial.body: [사설] 반도체 호황의 역설…증시는 더 취약해졌다, 오피니언
summary: 반도체 호황에도 증시는 취약성이 심화되고 있다.
한 산업 의존도 심화로 시장 리스크가 집중되었다.
구조적 개선 없이 단기 호황만으로는 한계가 있다.
editorial.stance: 반도체 의존도 심화는 경제 전체의 취약성을 초래하므로 구조 다각화가 시급하다.
editorial.titleTr: The Semiconductor Boom Paradox...Stock Market Grows More Fragile
summaryTr: Despite the semiconductor boom, stock market vulnerabilities are deepening.
Market risks have become concentrated due to intensifying dependence on a single industry.
There are limits to relying solely on short-term prosperity without structural improvements.

leanScore.label: Lean progressive
leanScore.rationale: 반도체 대기업 의존도 심화를 구조적 문제로 진단하고 경제 다각화를 요구하는 프레임은 재벌/대기업 집중 비판과 구조 개선을 지향하는 진보적 관점을 반영함.
